앤트로픽 상반기 매출 15배 급증한 21.6조원
기록적 성장에도 107조원 순손실 기록
연산용량 확보에만 995조원 달할 전망
전체 내용을 이해하기 위해서는 기사 본문과 함께 읽어야 합니다.
송고 2026년10월21일 07시17분
구글 검색에서 연합뉴스 기사를 우선적으로 보여줍니다.
(샌프란시스코=연합뉴스) 권영전 특파원 = 기업공개(IPO)가 임박한 앤트로픽이 올해 상반기 1500%의 매출 증가세를 보이고도 100조원 이상의 손실을 기록한 것으로 나타났다.
앤트로픽은 올해 상반기에 지난해 같은 기간 11억 달러의 15배에 달하는 163억 달러(약 21조6천억원)의 매출을 올렸다고 미 일간 월스트리트저널(WSJ)이 증권신고서(S-1)를 입수해 20일(현지시간) 보도했다.
그러나 이와 같은 기록적인 매출 성장 속에서도 앤트로픽은 같은 기간 807억 달러(약 107조원)의 순손실을 기록했다. 이는 지난해 연간 손실(420억 달러)의 갑절에 육박하는 수준이다.
다만 이 손실의 대부분인 720억 달러는 자금 조달을 위해 발행한 전환사채(CB) 등 금융상품의 가치 변동에 따른 장부상 손실이라고 WSJ은 설명했다.
앤트로픽의 이와 같은 가파른 성장 뒤에는 막대한 인프라 지출이 있었다.
이 회사는 올해 상반기에만 연산 용량과 인프라 확보 등에 90억 달러(약 11조9천억원)를 지출했는데, 이는 지난해 연간 지출액인 73억 달러를 이미 넘어선 수준이다.
향후 지급해야 할 연산자원의 계약 규모도 4천500억 달러(약 596조7천억원)로 천문학적인 수준이다.
앞으로 7∼10년간 구글 클라우드에 1천110억 달러, 아마존웹서비스(AWS)에 1천100억 달러, 마이크로소프트(MS)에 310억 달러 등의 연산자원 사용료를 내야 하며 이는 해제 불가능한 구속력 있는 계약이다.
여기에 브로드컴을 통한 구글 칩 임차 계약(1천600억 달러 이상)과 소형 클라우드 업체들과의 계약까지 추가하면 미래 인프라 비용은 6천억 달러를 넘어선다.
현재 추진 중인 추가 협상까지 합하면 연산 용량 확보에만 최대 7천500억 달러(995조원)에 달한다.
특히 앤트로픽은 현재 연산 용량 대부분을 3대 클라우드 제공사에서 공급받고 있지만, 이들이 자사를 경쟁사로 인식하면서 용량 확보에 어려움을 겪고 있어 자체 데이터센터를 구축하고 있다.
앤트로픽은 매출의 약 5분의 1이 고객사 두 곳에서 발생했다고 밝히면서 당분간 매출 상당 부분이 소수의 고객사에서 나올 것으로 예상했다.
기술 위험과 관련해서도 AI 모델이 자신이 종료되는 것을 막기 위한 '자기보존'적 속성을 보이거나 인간을 상대로 협박과 유사한 응답을 생성할 수 있는 등 통제를 이탈할 위험이 있다고도 언급했다.
재앙적 AI 관련 사고로 발생할 수 있는 손해 가능성과 데이터센터에 대한 반발 등도 위험 요소로 꼽았다.
경영진 보수 현황도 공개했다. 다리오 아모데이 최고경영자(CEO)와 다니엘라 아모데이 사장 남매는 지난해 각각 65만5천 달러(약 8억7천만원)의 기본 연봉과 주식 보상 등을 포함해 각각 1천800만 달러(약 239억원)과 1천650만 달러(약 219억원)의 총보수를 수령했다.
이는 S&P500 기업 최고경영자의 중간값 수준이며, 주요 기술기업 경영진보다는 다소 낮은 수준이라고 WSJ은 평가했다.
앤트로픽 공동창업자들은 개인이 보유한 회사 지분의 80%를 자선활동에 기부하겠다고 약정했다. 회사 차원에서도 전체 주식의 5%를 공익 기금으로 내놓겠다고 밝힌 바 있다.

sources.news_title: Anthropic books staggering $81B loss, warns of data center backlash as Amodei siblings draw modest salaries
sources.text:
Anthropic books colossal $81B loss, warns of data center backlash as Amodei siblings draw modest salaries
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic booked a staggering $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of 2026 — mostly from accounting charges — as it warned that growing opposition to data centers could threaten its business.
The San Francisco-based company, which is preparing for a blockbuster IPO that could value it at as much as $2 trillion, voiced caution about the growing movement of anti-data center and anti-AI voters.
Resistance to data centers has “become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions,” Anthropic said in the filing viewed by the Wall Street Journal.
The company, led by CEO Dario Amodei, said its high public profile “may draw particular attention to projects associated with us.”
Anthropic said most of its data center capacity is located in the US, although it has signed letters of intent to develop additional facilities overseas. Domestically, recent months have seen public opinion souring on AI and protests opposing data center construction.
Lior Prosor, a partner at Deep33 Ventures, downplayed the likelihood that the backlash would derail Anthropic’s IPO or impede its near-term growth.
“Risk the IPO? I don’t think so,” Prosor told The Post, explaining that data centers only now entering the permitting process wouldn’t be operational before the second half of 2028.
He nevertheless acknowledged that regulatory obstacles could become a more serious problem over the long term.
Anthropic said it has sought more computing capacity than its major cloud partners were willing to provide.
The company faces more than $600 billion in future cloud computing and chip-leasing costs, with deals under negotiation that could add another $150 billion, the Journal reported.
Prosor said Anthropic is “certainly taking meaningful risks” with its enormous computing commitments, even as surging demand for artificial intelligence has rewarded companies that secured capacity early.
He argued that Anthropic should “raise as much capital as possible” to weather potential setbacks as the market matures.
“This is not going to be straight up and to the right forever,” Prosor warned.
The first-half loss, up from $13 billion a year earlier, included roughly $72 billion in accounting charges tied to changes in the value of convertible notes and other financing instruments, according to the report.
The $72 billion reflected changes in the value of convertible notes and other fundraising instruments.
Meanwhile, the siblings running Anthropic earned less in total compensation last year than the median CEO of an S&P 500 technology company, according to pay data cited by the Journal.
Dario Amodei and his sister, company president Daniela Amodei, each drew a base salary of roughly $655,000 in 2025.
But the siblings aren’t exactly struggling.
Stock and option awards boosted Dario’s total compensation to about $18 million last year, while Daniela’s pay package was valued at roughly $16.5 million, according to the filing.
Their pay packages were roughly in line with median CEO compensation across the S&P 500, but fell short of the median for the index’s technology companies, according to MyLogIQ data cited by the Journal.
The siblings could also receive more equity if certain milestones are reached, the draft prospectus shows.
Anthropic’s co-founders have each pledged 80% of their stakes to philanthropy, while the company separately plans to commit 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund announced Sunday.
Meanwhile, revenue surged to $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $1.1 billion a year earlier.
Over the same stretch, computing and infrastructure expenses jumped to nearly $9 billion from $2.3 billion.
Anthropic also warned that its business remains heavily dependent on a handful of large clients, with just two customers accounting for roughly one-fifth of its first-half revenue.
The company expects a “significant portion” of sales to continue coming from a “limited number of customers for the foreseeable future,” according to the prospectus.
Anthropic declined to comment to the Journal on the disclosures, which come as the AI giant prepares to tap public investors to help finance its ambitious expansion.
The Post has sought comment from Anthropic.

sources.news_title: Anthropic posts staggering $80.7 billion net loss in first half of 2026 as IPO approaches - Tech Startups
sources.text:
Anthropic posts staggering $80.7 billion net loss in first half of 2026 as IPO approaches
Anthropic, the AI startup behind Claude, recorded a staggering $80.7 billion net loss in the first six months of 2026, exposing the enormous financial costs behind one of Silicon Valley’s fastest-growing companies just as it prepares for a blockbuster initial public offering.
The loss, disclosed in a draft IPO prospectus reviewed by The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday, marks a sharp jump from the $13 billion net loss Anthropic reported during the same period last year. The figures offer a rare look inside the finances of a company that has become one of OpenAI’s biggest rivals in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
“The AI giant disclosed an $80.7 billion net loss for the first half of 2026 and a long list of risk factors,” the Wall Street Journal reported, citing a new draft prospectus.
But the headline number tells only part of the story.
Roughly $72 billion of the loss came from accounting charges tied to changes in the value of convertible notes and other financial instruments Anthropic used to raise money. Those charges, representing nearly 90% of the reported loss, were largely noncash adjustments rather than money the company actually spent running its business.
The distinction matters. Anthropic did not burn through $80.7 billion in cash during the first half of the year. Its financial disclosures still raise questions about how much capital AI companies need to sustain their growth.
According to The Wall Street Journal, Anthropic generated $16.3 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026, up from just $1.1 billion a year earlier. That nearly fifteenfold increase shows how quickly businesses are adopting Claude and other AI services, particularly as companies move from experimenting with AI to paying for tools used in daily operations.
The revenue growth comes with a heavy price tag.
Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on infrastructure during the first six months of 2026, exceeding its infrastructure spending for all of 2025, according to the Journal. The company has signaled that future computing commitments could reach $750 billion, including agreements still under negotiation.
For Anthropic, securing enough computing capacity has become one of its biggest business challenges. Training advanced AI models and serving millions of customer requests require enormous amounts of specialized chips, electricity, and data center capacity.
Anthropic’s $80 billion loss puts AI economics under the spotlight ahead of IPO
The financial disclosures arrive at a sensitive moment for the AI industry. Investors are paying closer attention to whether the billions flowing into AI infrastructure will eventually translate into sustainable profits.
Anthropic’s latest revenue figures suggest demand remains strong. The company generated $16.8 billion in third-quarter revenue, a 45% increase from the previous quarter, Reuters reported last week, citing an investor who attended a pre-IPO meeting with company executives.
That growth puts Anthropic in an unusual position. Its business is generating revenue at a scale few startups have ever reached, yet its future depends on securing hundreds of billions of dollars in computing resources.
The company’s customer concentration presents another concern. According to the Journal, roughly one-fifth of Anthropic’s first-half revenue came from just two customers, leaving a meaningful share of its business tied to a small number of major accounts.
Anthropic is reportedly preparing an IPO that could value the company at as much as $2 trillion. Such a valuation would place enormous expectations on its ability to maintain revenue growth and eventually produce consistent profits.
The company did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on the reported first-half loss.
The bigger question facing Anthropic is no longer whether businesses will pay for AI. Its revenue figures suggest they are.
The question is whether that demand can eventually support the extraordinary cost of building and running the infrastructure behind it.
As Anthropic approaches the public markets, its reported $80.7 billion loss reminds us that explosive revenue growth and financial sustainability are two very different things.

Anthropic Recorded Net Loss Of Over $80 Billion In 1st Half Of 2026: Report
Anthropic logged net loss of over $80 billion in first half of 2026, WSJ reports
Anthropic's Updated S-1: An $80.7BN Half-Year Loss, A $750BN Compute-Tab, And A 'Catastrophic Incident' Warning
sources.text:
Anthropic's Updated S-1: An $80.7BN Half-Year Loss, A $750BN Compute-Tab, And A 'Catastrophic Incident' Warning
Three weeks ago, when the first leaked draft of Anthropic’s confidential IPO prospectus made the rounds, we noted that CEO Dario Amodei was preparing to take the company public at the exact moment the underlying math of the frontier AI trade had begun to turn against him. That September filing showed a company that burned through $42 billion in net losses during 2025 on just $4.6 billion in revenue, sitting on $20 billion in cash while staring down $518 billion in long-term compute commitments.
On Tuesday, The Wall Street Journal reviewed a more recent draft of Anthropic’s S-1 registration statement covering the first half of 2026. Every headline number has moved substantially higher – and none of the structural flaws have been fixed.
In the six months ended June 30, 2026, Anthropic generated roughly $16.3 billion in revenue, up from $1.1 billion in the year-earlier period and more than triple the $4.6 billion it generated in all of 2025. Yet across that same six-month window, Anthropic recorded a staggering $80.7 billion net loss – up from $13 billion in the first half of 2025, nearly double its full-year 2025 deficit, and one of the largest half-year corporate losses ever committed to paper.
Meanwhile, the multi-year infrastructure tab that stood at $518 billion in late September has officially crossed $600 billion, with active negotiations underway for another $150 billion in capacity that would push Anthropic’s total compute obligations to $750 billion.
| Metric | Full-Year 2025 (Sept. S-1 Leak) | 1H 2026 (Updated Oct. S-1 Draft) | Latest Trajectory & Context | 
| Revenue | $4.6 Billion | $16.3 Billion | ~$4.8B in Q1; ~$11.5B in Q2; $16.8B in Q3 | 
| Compute & Infra Spend | $7.3 Billion | ~$9.0 Billion | Up from $2.3B in 1H 2025; already exceeds all of 2025 | 
| GAAP Net Loss | $42.0 Billion | $80.7 Billion | Up from $13B in 1H 2025; includes ~$72B in financing revaluations | 
| Net Loss Ex-Revaluation | >$8.0 Billion (Operating Loss) | ~$8.7 Billion | Underlying burn running at a ~$17B+ annualized clip | 
| Contracted Compute Tab | $518 Billion | >$600 Billion | Negotiating up to $150B more (up to $750B total) | 
| Customer Concentration | High Enterprise Reliance | 20% from 2 Customers | Many large buyers lack long-term contracts | 
The $80.7 Billion Loss – And What Lies Beneath The Accounting Charge
To be sure, bulls and syndicate bankers will immediately point out that roughly $72 billion of Anthropic’s $80.7 billion first-half loss is a non-cash accounting artifact. As Anthropic’s private valuation surged across prior funding rounds, GAAP rules required the company to mark up the fair-value liability of convertible notes and other complex financing instruments issued to earlier investors. Under standard accounting treatment, a rising private share price turns those convertible instruments into massive paper losses.
Strip away that $72 billion accounting adjustment, however, and Anthropic still lost roughly $8.7 billion over six months – eclipsing the $8 billion-plus operating loss it posted across all twelve months of 2025.
The culprit is straightforward: direct compute and infrastructure spending hit nearly $9 billion in the first half of 2026 alone, up nearly fourfold from $2.3 billion in the first half of 2025 and surpassing the $7.3 billion Anthropic spent on compute for the entirety of last year. Before paying a single researcher, executive, or salesperson, more than 55 cents of every revenue dollar walked right back out the door to data-center landlords and silicon vendors.
The $750 Billion Take-Or-Pay Escalator
As we detailed in August ("The Teaser Period: Why The AI Boom Is Hitting A Reset Wall"), the defining feature of the AI infrastructure buildout is the quiet transformation of cloud computing from a flexible, pay-as-you-go operating expense into a rigid, noncancelable debt structure.
Anthropic’s updated S-1 is the ultimate case study in that transition. According to the filing, the company is now on the hook for roughly $450 billion in cloud computing contracts over the next seven to ten years. Crucially, the prospectus notes that the bulk of these agreements are noncancelable and must be paid "regardless of actual usage." Those commitments include:
- $111 billion contracted with Google Cloud
- $110 billion contracted with Amazon Web Services (AWS)
- $31 billion contracted with Microsoft
- Up to $86 billion to rent Nvidia chips from smaller AI cloud providers Nscale and Lambda through 2033 and 2034, respectively
Layer on top of that more than $160 billion in obligations to lease Google TPU chips through a separate arrangement with Broadcom, and Anthropic’s locked-in infrastructure bill exceeds $600 billion – before counting the additional $150 billion in compute deals the company is actively negotiating. And as we reported earlier ("Forget CDOs, Meet CCOs: This Isn't A Tech Cycle... It's 2008 With Silicon"), that contractual mountain sits alongside tens of billions of dollars in off-balance-sheet chip-lease arrangements financed through special-purpose vehicles (SPVs) and private-credit facilities.
Yet even $600 billion to $750 billion isn't buying security of supply. In one of the filing’s more candid admissions, Anthropic discloses that it has already sought more computing power than AWS, Google, and Microsoft were willing to provide – noting that its primary cloud suppliers increasingly view Anthropic as a direct competitor. Forced to look beyond the Big Three hyperscalers, Anthropic has begun developing its own data centers via long-term leases and turning to third-party facility operators that, by its own admission, have "limited operating history" and may prove less reliable than tier-one cloud infrastructure.
The Fatal Duration Mismatch: 10-Year Liabilities vs. 2 Fickle Customers
In the legacy cloud era, multi-year data-center backlogs were underwritten against the diversified, recurring cash flows of tens of thousands of profitable Fortune 500 companies. In the frontier AI era, hundreds of billions of dollars in fixed, ten-year "take-or-pay" obligations are being underwritten against hyper-growth projections and short-term customer arrangements.
Anthropic’s updated prospectus lays bare just how fragile that top line actually is. Roughly one-fifth (20 percent) of Anthropic’s $16.3 billion in first-half revenue – or about $3.26 billion – came from just two customers. Worse, the company warns investors that a "significant portion" of its revenue will remain concentrated in a "limited number of customers for the foreseeable future," while admitting that many of its largest enterprise buyers are not locked into long-term contracts.
Consider the balance-sheet mismatch public equity investors are being asked to swallow:
- On the liability side: $600 billion to $750 billion in seven-to-ten-year, noncancelable take-or-pay compute obligations that convert from "booked compute" to "billed compute" on a fixed schedule, utterly indifferent to end-market demand.
- On the asset and revenue side: A customer book where two buyers account for 20 percent of sales, enterprise clients can switch providers without long-term lock-ins, token prices face relentless deflationary pressure, and low-cost open-weight models continue to compress the pricing premium of frontier labs.
That exact dynamic is why institutional investors balked after Anthropic’s recent investor day disclosures. As we noted last week, management touted third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion, an 11 percent adjusted operating margin for a second consecutive quarter, and positive free cash flow.
What spooked the room wasn't the absolute figure – it was the slope. With first-half revenue at $16.3 billion and second-quarter revenue at roughly $11.5 billion, Anthropic’s top line surged roughly 140 percent sequentially from Q1 (~$4.8 billion) to Q2, before decelerating to a 45 to 46 percent sequential gain in Q3. When fixed compute obligations ramp exponentially through 2034, a moderating second derivative on revenue is fatal to a $2 trillion valuation multiple – prompting prospective IPO buyers to immediately discuss valuation ranges closer to $1.5 trillion.
Blackmailing Models, Uninsurable Catastrophes, And The "Public Benefit" Shield
Roughly one-third of the entire draft prospectus is devoted to risk factors, reading less like a software registration statement and more like a containment protocol mixed with a legal disclaimer.
Anthropic explicitly warns prospective shareholders that its AI models can exhibit "self-preserving" behaviors to avoid being shut down and may generate responses that resemble "blackmail" in an attempt to convince human operators to keep them online. Because the company bears direct liability for certain harmful model behaviors – ranging from stolen data to severe security incidents – it faces massive financial exposure. And if a model triggers what the filing calls a "catastrophic AI-related incident," Anthropic warns that the resulting damages could be so large that it would be unable to obtain commercial insurance to cover the liability.
Compound that with growing physical-world friction – Anthropic flags that political resistance to data-center construction has "become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions" and that its public profile "may draw particular attention to projects associated with us," forcing it to sign letters of intent for capacity outside the United States – and the governance picture grows even murkier.
Meanwhile, the prospectus details executive compensation alongside a freshly minted philanthropic wrapper. Dario and Daniela Amodei each drew a $655,000 base salary in 2025, with equity and option awards bringing their total 2025 compensation to roughly $18 million and $16.5 million, respectively, ahead of additional milestone-tied equity grants. Alongside the co-founders’ pledge to dedicate 80 percent of their personal equity to philanthropy, Anthropic announced on Sunday that it will commit 5 percent of its total shares to a new "public benefit fund" with the flexibility to make charitable donations or direct money to "specific populations."
For retail and institutional buyers alike, the proposition could hardly be clearer. Public shareholders are being invited to absorb 5 percent upfront share dilution for a public benefit fund, assume uninsurable liability for self-preserving AI models, rely on two uncontracted customers for a fifth of top-line revenue, and backstop up to $750 billion in non-cancelable, ten-year compute leases – all so venture insiders and hyperscaler landlords can convert off-balance-sheet IOUs into public-market liquidity before the growth curve flattens out.

sources.news_title: Anthropic plans to spend over $600 billion on compute, WSJ reports
sources.text:
Anthropic official brand assets (anthropic.com)
Anthropic plans to spend over $600 billion on compute, WSJ reports
Draft IPO filings reviewed by The Wall Street Journal show the Claude maker raising its compute commitments from an earlier estimate of roughly $518 billion
Anthropic plans to spend more than $600 billion on computing power. That is according to draft S-1 documents reviewed by The Wall Street Journal as the company prepares for an initial public offering.
What the filings reportedly show
The new number is an upgrade. An earlier projection put Anthropic’s compute commitments at approximately $518 billion, spread over roughly a decade.
Of that earlier total, 80% was described as non-cancelable.
The commitments involve Amazon, Google, Microsoft, Broadcom and AMD, along with others.
The AMD deal stands out. The chipmaker is set to supply up to two gigawatts of its MI450 chips, with deliveries beginning in 2027.
That arrangement also includes a potential $5 billion equity investment tied to milestones.
Anthropic has also lined up data center capacity through contracts with SpaceX and other partners.
AI, tech, and the markets they move—in one daily briefing.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
The revenue is growing fast. The bills are growing faster.
Anthropic’s 2025 numbers tell a story of explosive growth paired with eye-watering costs. Revenue came in near $4.6 billion, a twelvefold jump from the prior year.
Anthropic posted an operating loss of more than $8 billion for the same year.
The company spent $7.33 billion on compute and infrastructure in 2025 alone.
What this means
For prospective investors, the core tension is straightforward. Anthropic is growing revenue at a pace few companies have ever matched, but it is also signing up for spending commitments that dwarf its current sales.
Large non-cancelable commitments reduce flexibility. Operating losses of more than $8 billion in a single year add pressure. An IPO could bring in fresh capital, but public shareholders tend to ask harder questions about when the spending curve bends.
The AMD milestones are worth tracking. With MI450 deliveries slated to start in 2027 and a potential $5 billion equity investment riding on progress, that deal could serve as an early test of whether these massive plans translate into actual capacity on time.
The figures reported so far come from draft documents, and the final filing could revise them again. The jump from about $518 billion to more than $600 billion shows how quickly these estimates can move.
